intro: ‘Hawthorne’ is the second movement of Ives’s Piano Sonata No. 2, ‘Concord, Mass., 1840–60’, a scherzo drawn from Hawthorne’s stories, with frost on a window, a train to heaven and a hymn interrupted by a circus. It ranges from clusters on the black keys to ragtime played with the fists.

sections.label: Intro · Rapid piano arpeggios
sections.mNote: Rapid piano figures open the Hawthorne movement.

sections.label: A · Soft clusters above a melody
sections.mNote: Clusters of adjacent black keys sound high above a slower tune.

sections.label: B · Rag with displaced accents
sections.mNote: Fast syncopations run against the piano’s beat

sections.label: C · Hymn interrupting the ragtime
sections.mNote: The quiet tune is the hymn Martyn.

sections.label: D · March, ragtime and clusters
sections.mNote: A march leads to the main climax in clusters

sections.label: E · Columbia, fragments, left hand
sections.mNote: The left hand plays fragments of the patriotic song.

sections.label: F · Columbia theme, longer phrases
sections.mNote: Longer phrases follow the piano’s interruptions.

sections.label: Coda · fast triplets across the keyboard
sections.mNote: Fragments of tunes appear in the fast closing passage

cues.title: Opening arpeggios
cues.text: The piano opens with rapid arpeggios. Ives linked the opening to the children in Hawthorne’s The Three Golden Apples, waking to frost on the window. The arpeggios soon lead into railway music.
cues.evidence: Kyle Gann, “Following the Concord Sonata”, “Hawthorne”: Ives’s identification of the opening arpeggios with the frosted window and the following railway music. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Felt-covered board clusters
cues.text: In the first slow episode, the score calls for a felt-covered board, fifteen inches long, to press neighbouring black keys high on the piano. The clusters sound softly while a slower melody moves below.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: first slow episode, fifteen-inch felt-covered board, high black-key clusters and lower melody. This describes the score’s technique; the recording credits do not specify Liang’s implement. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ives on the Hawthorne movement
cues.text: In his essay, Ives wrote that any full picture of Hawthorne rests on the influence of sin upon the conscience. He described the movement as an “extended fragment” drawn from Hawthorne’s wilder, fantastical adventures into half-childlike, half-fairylike realms, and it does not attempt that fuller picture.
cues.evidence: Charles Ives, Essays Before a Sonata (1920), “Hawthorne”, final two paragraphs. https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3673/3673-h/3673-h.htm#hawthorne

cues.title: Fast rag
cues.text: The slow melody gives way to a fast rag. Accents fall just before the beat, in ragtime syncopation. Ives keeps changing the tunes while the accents remain displaced.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: fast rag after the cluster episode and Ives’s use of ragtime syncopation. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hawthorne’s story, 1843
cues.text: Hawthorne’s The Celestial Rail-Road, published in 1843, turns Bunyan’s arduous pilgrimage into a comfortable train ride, and the passengers can stow their sins with the luggage. Ives’s scherzo takes the bustle of the train and the irreverence of the story.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”, summarises the story, its publication date and its place in Ives’s scherzo. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

cues.title: Hymn tune Martyn
cues.text: The rag is interrupted by the hymn Martyn, associated with the words “Jesus, lover of my soul”. Its shape resembles the sonata’s recurring melody. The rag returns, and the hymn interrupts it a second time.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: two Martyn quotations interrupt the rag; the hymn’s opening words and resemblance to the human-faith melody. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hawthorne essay, 1920
cues.text: In the “Hawthorne” essay of 1920, Ives described an old hymn heard in a churchyard while a circus parade came down Main Street. In his account, the hymn sheltered the people among the graves from the noise of the parade.
cues.evidence: Charles Ives, Essays Before a Sonata (1920), “Hawthorne”, final paragraph: the churchyard hymn and circus parade. https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3673/3673-h/3673-h.htm#hawthorne

cues.title: March and second ragtime
cues.text: A march breaks off from the ragtime, with piano clusters imitating drums. It slows to a pause, and a longer rag begins. This passage builds to the climax of fist clusters.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: the march, drum-like clusters, pause and renewed ragtime ending in the fist-cluster climax. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Childhood drum lessons
cues.text: Ives liked to tell how his father found him, aged five, banging out his band’s drum parts on the piano with his fists. George Ives told Charles that this was all right if he knew what he was doing, and sent him down the street for drum lessons.
cues.evidence: Jan Swafford, “Ives The Man: His Life”, Charles Ives Society, recounting a story Ives told. https://charlesives.org/ives-man-his-life. Gann ties the movement’s drum-like clusters to the story: https://charlesives.org/node/6616

cues.title: Phrases of Columbia, left hand
cues.text: After the cluster climax, the piano starts again slowly. The left hand plays phrases of Columbia, the Gem of the Ocean.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: the slow restart after the fist clusters and Columbia phrases in the left hand. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Columbia, the Gem of the Ocean
cues.text: Columbia, the Gem of the Ocean becomes more recognisable as its phrases accumulate. Fragments of the tune appear across the piano before the tune is heard whole, which reverses the usual order of theme and variations.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: progressive recognition of Columbia, discussed through J. Peter Burkholder’s term cumulative form. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ives’s essay on Hawthorne, 1920
cues.text: At the end of his Hawthorne essay Ives listed what the music may recall: frost on a window, Feathertop, the Seven Vagabonds and Phoebe’s Garden. He then qualified the list with the words “not something that happens, but the way something happens”.
cues.evidence: Ives, Essays Before a Sonata (1920), final paragraph of “Hawthorne”: https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3673/3673-h/3673-h.htm#hawthorne

cues.title: Triplet figures and final bars
cues.text: Rapid triplet figures run across the keyboard and carry fragments of familiar tunes. Near the end, Columbia and the hymn appear for the last time, followed by a final gesture across the whole piano.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”, final paragraph: complex triplet figures, Columbia references, hymn reminiscence and closing joke. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Black-key cluster above a slow melody
transitions.to: A · Soft clusters above a melody
transitions.how: The rapid piano figures stop. In the slow episode, neighbouring black keys sound softly high on the keyboard, pressed down together with a felt-covered board. A languid melody moves beneath the cluster at a different pace from the opening arpeggios.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: opening arpeggios and first slow cluster episode. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: Cluster passage to fast rag
transitions.from: A · Soft clusters above a melody
transitions.how: The soft high clusters and slow lower melody give way to fast ragtime. Accented notes fall before the beat, which displaces the accents. Quick, sharply articulated phrases replace the held black-key chords.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: the fast rag follows the slow cluster passage; his discussion explains its displaced accents. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: Martyn quotations interrupt the rag
transitions.how: The piano’s ragtime breaks off for a quiet statement of the hymn Martyn. The hymn’s longer notes resemble the sonata’s recurring melody. The rag then resumes, and a second quiet statement of Martyn follows it.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: two quiet Martyn quotations interrupt the rag. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: From the rag into a march
transitions.how: The third continuation of the rag breaks off abruptly into a march. Clusters in the piano imitate drum strokes beneath the march. The march slows to a pause, and a longer ragtime passage follows, building to the fist-cluster climax.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: the third rag continuation, march, pause and renewed ragtime. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: Fist clusters to Columbia phrases
transitions.how: The long ragtime passage builds to clusters played with the fists. After them the piano starts again slowly, and the left hand plays phrases of Columbia, the Gem of the Ocean. The song is introduced a phrase at a time.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: fist-cluster climax, slow restart and Columbia phrases in the left hand. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: Left-hand fragments of Columbia lengthen
transitions.how: The scraps of Columbia, the Gem of the Ocean in the left hand are developed into longer, more recognisable phrases. As the tune becomes clearer, the surrounding texture increases in speed and force. Interruptions continue to break up its course.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: the late cumulative treatment of Columbia. The existing section boundary divides this extended passage. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: Triplet figuration after Columbia
transitions.to: Coda · fast triplets across the keyboard
transitions.how: After the passage built on Columbia, complex triplet figures take over the piano. Fragments of tunes pass through the running notes. The triplet motion continues up to the last recalls of the patriotic song and the hymn.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”, closing paragraph: the triplet whirlwind and final tune references. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

sources.locator: Introduction calls Hawthorne a scherzo; the Hawthorne essay’s final paragraphs distinguish the novelist’s moral subject matter from the fantastic realm attempted by this movement. The modern prefatory biographical sketch is not used as Ives’s testimony.

composer.epithet: Composer and New York life-insurance salesman whose music sets a hymn heard across a river against a marching band.
facts: His father George Ives; Horatio Parker at Yale, 1894–98
Church organist until 1902; insurance executive at Ives & Myrick
Concord Sonata and Essays Before a Sonata, 1920; 114 Songs, 1922
Danbury bands and hymn singing; the New England of Emerson and Thoreau
composer.background:
George Ives played his cornet across a pond so that his son could hear what distance did to the sound. He made the boy sing in one key while he accompanied in another, built instruments that could play quarter-tones and tried out the collision of two marching bands. A former Union Army bandmaster, he earned his living teaching and directing music in Danbury, Connecticut, where his son Charles was born in 1874.

The lessons also involved work. By fourteen Charles was a salaried church organist; at seventeen he wrote the Variations on America, a set of variations for keyboard on the tune of God Save the King. At Yale, which he entered in 1894, Horatio Parker taught him counterpoint, orchestration and the construction of a symphony. His First Symphony, written in a European idiom, came out of that teaching. George died of a stroke during Charles’s first term.
